label.reasoning: The question focuses on relationships among displacement, velocity, and acceleration in one-dimensional motion, using integration to obtain position and differentiation to obtain acceleration.
The question tests the calculus relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration for one-dimensional motion, including integration with an initial condition and differentiation of velocity.

Both parts assess the impulse–momentum theorem, including integrating a time-dependent force, interpreting the area under a force–time graph, and relating initial rest to final momentum. These are core Unit 4 concepts.

The central task is deriving the angular frequency of small oscillations. It requires relating potential energy to force, identifying stable equilibria, and applying Newton’s second law to obtain the approximate SHM equation.

The central task is deriving the angular frequency of small oscillations. It requires relating potential energy to force, assessing equilibrium stability, and applying Newton’s second law to identify the approximate simple harmonic motion.
Both parts focus on the impulse-momentum theorem, interpreting the area under a force-time graph as change in momentum, and using zero initial momentum to relate total impulse to final momentum.

The question centers on Newton’s second law for rotation, relating time-dependent torque to angular acceleration and interpreting the resulting angular velocity graph, including its initial slope and long-time asymptote.

The item applies Newton’s second law for rotation to connect time-dependent torque with angular acceleration and the slope of an angular-velocity graph, including its initial slope and long-time behavior.

The item focuses on interpreting a velocity–time graph through its slope and enclosed area to describe acceleration and position. It also compares average and instantaneous velocity. All required content is kinematics.

The item emphasizes interpreting a velocity–time graph through its slope and area to describe acceleration and position. It also compares average and instantaneous velocity. All required concepts belong to kinematics.

The item concerns a physical pendulum’s period and the limits of the small-angle approximation. Relating the restoring torque–angle slope to the period requires torque and rotational dynamics, together with physical-pendulum and SHM concepts.

The item concerns physical-pendulum periods and the small-angle approximation. It requires gravitational force, restoring torque and rotational dynamics, and the connection between linear restoring behavior and simple harmonic motion.

The item centers on testing a velocity-proportional resistive force and its predicted time constant. Kinematics supports measuring speed and its time dependence; force dynamics connects drag, acceleration, mass, and the validity of the linear-drag model.

The item centers on testing the impulse-momentum theorem by comparing the area under a force-time graph with the measured change in momentum. Identifying experimental variables and controlling other interactions supports this Unit 4 concept.

The item centers on potential-energy extrema and curvature as criteria for equilibrium and stability. Force and translational dynamics are also needed to interpret restoring forces, design a stability test, and explain why friction does not invalidate the stability criterion.

The item focuses on testing velocity-proportional resistive forces and interpreting their characteristic time constant. Kinematics supports speed-versus-time measurements, while resistive-force models and Newton’s second law connect drag, mass, and the time constant.

The item centers on potential-energy equilibria and stability through potential curvature. Connecting potential gradients to restoring forces, interpreting the resulting motion, and explaining friction’s role also require force and translational dynamics.

The item centers on designing an experimental test of the impulse–momentum theorem, interpreting the area under a force–time graph as impulse, and accounting for momentum changes from other interactions.

Both parts assess rotational inertia: how it scales with rod length at fixed mass and how a nonuniform mass distribution determines the numerical prefactor. These concepts fall within rotational inertia in Unit 5.
Both parts focus on rotational inertia: how it scales with rod length at fixed mass and how a nonuniform mass distribution determines the numerical prefactor through distance-squared weighting.

The item centers on testing Newton’s second law for rotation and using a time-dependent net torque to predict angular velocity. Measurement design, rotational kinematics, moment of inertia, and negligible bearing torque are all addressed within Unit 5.

The item tests rotational Newton’s second law through experimental design, the effect of negligible bearing torque, and angular velocity predicted from a time-dependent torque. Rotational dynamics and rotational kinematics are sufficient; angular momentum methods are not required.

The question concerns the calculus relationships among velocity, position, and acceleration in one-dimensional motion, and how integration and differentiation preserve proportionality to a parameter. Only kinematics is required.

The item tests relationships among velocity, position, and acceleration through integration and differentiation, including how these operations preserve proportionality to a parameter. Only kinematics is required.

The question centers on velocity-dependent drag and how its coefficient affects motion. Newton’s second law determines the velocity’s time dependence, while kinematics connects velocity to displacement and total stopping distance.

The question centers on velocity-dependent resistive forces and how drag strength affects motion. Newton’s second law determines the decay timescale, while kinematic relationships between velocity, time, and displacement determine the total stopping distance.

The item primarily assesses two-dimensional projectile kinematics, including vector functions, motion graphs, flight time, and range. Determining radius of curvature from normal acceleration also requires the circular-motion relationship covered in Unit 2.

Quadratic fluid drag is the central concept. Newton’s second law determines the differential equation and terminal speed, while kinematics relates velocity and acceleration and supports interpreting their time-dependent graphs and limits.

The item primarily assesses two-dimensional projectile motion, including vector equations, motion graphs, flight time, and range. Finding the radius of curvature from normal acceleration also requires the circular-motion relationship between speed, acceleration, and radius.

The item centers on circular motion, requiring a free-body diagram and Newton’s second law in vertical and radial directions. Circular-motion kinematics connects path radius, angular speed, and orbital period.

The central concept is quadratic fluid drag, analyzed using Newton’s second law to model terminal speed and time-dependent motion. Kinematics is also required to relate acceleration to velocity and interpret their graphs and limiting values.
The question requires integrating a position-dependent force to find work, then applying the work–energy theorem to determine the particle’s final speed from rest.
The question requires integrating a position-dependent force to find work, then applying the work–energy theorem to determine the particle’s final speed from rest. Both are Unit 3 concepts.

The item tests an inverse-square central-force model and distinguishes it from another radial force law. Newton’s second law connects measured acceleration to force, allowing the radial dependence to be tested without knowing the force constant.

The item tests an inverse-square central-force model characteristic of gravitation. Analyzing position and acceleration data requires kinematics, while connecting acceleration to the proposed force law requires Newton’s second law.

The item centers on uniform circular motion: resolving string tension into vertical and radial components, applying Newton’s second law, and relating centripetal acceleration to angular speed and orbital period. Despite the pendulum-like setup, no oscillation occurs.
The question centers on integrating a time-dependent force to obtain impulse and momentum change. Long-time momentum and direction reversal follow from the resulting momentum function and its sign.

All parts use the impulse–momentum theorem to relate a time-dependent force to momentum changes. Direction reversal follows from the momentum changing sign, and the finite total impulse is determined by the convergence of the force integral.

An elastic collision requires component-wise conservation of linear momentum and conservation of translational kinetic energy. Vector decomposition and two-dimensional velocity geometry are needed to relate outgoing directions and speed magnitudes.

An elastic collision requires conservation of linear momentum in two dimensions and translational kinetic energy. Vector components and outgoing velocity directions require kinematics concepts, while the central topic is elastic collisions.

The item analyzes measured oscillations to estimate effective stiffness, predict and compare periods, and identify departures from harmonic behavior. It requires restoring-force and spring-force concepts plus SHM analysis; energy calculations are not necessary.

The item centers on analyzing oscillation data and identifying the limits of the harmonic approximation. Spring-force behavior determines the effective spring constant, while SHM theory connects it to the period and supports comparison across amplitudes. Potential-energy calculations are not required because the restoring force is directly measurable.

The item requires comparing total linear momentum and translational kinetic energy before and after a collision to test momentum conservation and classify elasticity, with measurement uncertainties propagated into both comparisons.

The analysis compares total linear momentum and translational kinetic energy before and after the collision to test momentum conservation and classify elasticity. Measurement uncertainties must be propagated into both comparisons.
Locating the beam’s center of mass requires translational force balance and rotational torque balance. Adding known masses tests the inferred location through predicted changes in the sensor forces.

Locating and validating the beam’s center of mass requires translational force balance and rotational equilibrium, using measured support forces, torque balance, and the effects of added known masses.

The question concerns circular satellite orbits and escape energy. It requires circular-motion dynamics and gravitation, translational kinetic and gravitational potential energy, energy conservation, and the kinematic relationship between orbital speed, radius, and period.

The item centers on orbiting satellites, requiring circular-motion dynamics and gravitation, translational kinetic and gravitational potential energy, and escape energy. Relating orbital speed, radius, and period also requires kinematics.

The question centers on angular impulse and its relationship to change in angular momentum. Rotational inertia and the connection between angular momentum and angular velocity are needed to determine the final rotation and assess reversal.

The item centers on rolling without slipping, combining gravitational potential energy, translational and rotational kinetic energy, rotational inertia, and the linear–angular speed relationship. Explaining why static friction does no work also requires friction and work concepts.

Rolling without slipping combines conservation of mechanical energy, translational and rotational kinetic energy, rotational inertia, and the linear–angular speed relationship. Explaining why static friction does no work also requires understanding static friction and work at the contact point.

The item centers on testing rotational work-energy using torque versus angular position and changes in rotational kinetic energy. It also requires rotational kinematics, rotational inertia, instantaneous rotational power, and identifying frictional torque through discrepancies in the energy accounting.

The question centers on angular impulse from a time-dependent torque and its relationship to change in angular momentum. Relating angular momentum to angular velocity determines the final rotation and reversal condition.

The item uses conservation of oscillator energy to relate velocity and position, then represents that relationship in phase space. It requires kinematic concepts, kinetic and potential energy, and simple harmonic motion.

The central task tests rotational work against changes in rotational kinetic energy. Angular motion and torque require Unit 5, while instantaneous-power comparisons require Unit 3. Controls and friction diagnostics support the rotational work-energy analysis.

The item centers on using oscillator energy to relate velocity and position, then representing SHM in phase space. It requires kinematic interpretation of position and velocity, kinetic and potential energy conservation, and properties of simple harmonic motion.

Conservation of mechanical energy determines speed, maximum speed, turning points, and whether the particle crosses the origin. Equilibrium and stability require relating force to the derivative of potential energy and analyzing the force near equilibrium.

The item centers on velocity-dependent resistive forces, requiring force diagrams and Newton’s second law to formulate and solve the motion equation. Kinematics is also required to derive acceleration and interpret velocity and acceleration graphs, including slopes, asymptotes, and concavity.

Velocity-dependent resistive force is the central topic. Newton’s second law and force diagrams establish the governing equation and terminal speed; kinematics connects velocity and acceleration and supports interpreting slopes, asymptotes, and concavity of their time graphs.

Conservation of mechanical energy determines speed, maximum speed, crossing, and turning points. Equilibrium and stability require relating potential energy to force and analyzing the force near equilibrium. The motion is not necessarily simple harmonic.
The item applies conservation of energy to a spring–mass oscillator, relating elastic potential energy to maximum kinetic energy and examining how maximum speed scales with oscillation amplitude.
The question uses conservation of energy to relate spring potential energy to maximum kinetic energy in a simple harmonic oscillator and asks how maximum speed scales with oscillation amplitude.

The central task applies rotational Newton’s second law to determine inertia. It also requires translational Newton’s second law for the hanging mass, acceleration measurements and kinematics, and the no-slip connection between linear and angular acceleration. Linearization, uncertainty, axle friction, and radius bias extend this model.

The item assesses the calculus relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration in one-dimensional motion: integrating velocity to obtain position and differentiating velocity to obtain acceleration.

The model combines translational and rotational Newton’s second laws with the no-slip acceleration constraint. Trials require measuring acceleration from motion data. Determining rotational inertia, diagnosing axle-friction torque, and assessing radius-dependent systematic error center on rotational dynamics.

The item tests the calculus relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration in one-dimensional motion: integrating velocity to obtain position and differentiating velocity to obtain acceleration.

The central topic is vertical circular motion, using radial Newton’s second law to analyze tension and the minimum speed for a taut string. Conservation of mechanical energy is also required to determine the speed at the bottom.

The item centers on vertical circular motion, requiring Newton’s second law and radial force analysis to determine string tension and minimum speed. Conservation of mechanical energy is needed to relate speeds at the top and bottom.

The item centers on calculating work from a position-dependent force and applying the work-energy theorem to determine speed and maximum kinetic energy. All parts require work and translational kinetic energy concepts from Unit 3.

The question centers on integrating a position-dependent force to determine work, applying the work-energy theorem to find speed, and identifying maximum kinetic energy from the sign of the force. These tasks require Unit 3 work and kinetic energy concepts.

The item centers on energy conservation with nonconservative work, connecting spring potential energy, frictional work, and translational kinetic energy. Unit 2 is required to determine kinetic friction from the normal force; Unit 3 supplies work and energy principles, including thermal energy dissipation.

The item centers on energy accounting with nonconservative friction, relating spring potential energy, frictional work, and translational kinetic energy. Unit 2 is required to determine kinetic friction from the normal force; Unit 3 supplies work, energy, and energy conservation.
